name: Timeular
tagline: Track time with projects and reminders using software-only controls

tiers.name: Personal
tiers.limits: 1 project budget; time tracking and reports.
tiers.notes: Timeular is now branded EARLY; annual total $90.

tiers.name: Personal Pro
tiers.limits: Up to 50 project budgets; rounding options of 1, 5, 6, 10, 15, or 30 minutes.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Team features; dedicated success manager at 20+ seats.

pricing.hiddenCosts: Taxes/VAT are extra and checkout localizes pricing; Team success-manager service starts only at 20+ seats.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Timeular, track time with projects and reminders using software-only controls. The hard boundary is physical tracker option, mobile apps, calendar integration, team features, and sync, plus ubiquitous capture, coaching, and team workflow.
coreLoopDIY: Track time and focused sessions with projects and reminders using software-only controls, review patterns locally, and export a transparent activity record.
requirements: optional accessibility permission for app-name tracking
whatYouLose: physical tracker option, mobile apps, calendar integration, team features, and sync
moatNotes: ubiquitous capture, coaching, and team workflow
ongoingBurden: idle detection, permissions, app metadata, privacy, notifications, sync, reports, integrations, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Timeular because the timer is simple, but people pay for frictionless capture and a history they trust enough to invoice or change habits from. The recurring cost buys idle detection, permissions, app metadata, privacy, notifications, sync, reports, integrations, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Kimai
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source time-tracking application with projects, reports, and exports.

alternatives.name: Clockify Free
alternatives.desc: Five users get timers, projects and PDF reports one month at a time; CSV, billable rates and approvals are paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup; install the Windows/macOS/Linux desktop app for automatic activity tracking
facts.dataFormat: Saved time entries, projects and reports live in Clockify's cloud; raw auto-tracker app and website activity stays in a local desktop database and is uploaded only when converted into a time entry
facts.gapVsPaid: It lacks Timeular's physical Tracker workflow and its more focused combination of reminders, automatic evidence and personal time-management coaching.
facts.setupBlocker: An account is required, and automatic tracking needs the desktop app plus operating-system activity permissions

alternatives.name: My Hours Free
alternatives.desc: A clean five-person timer with unlimited projects, clients and basic reports; approvals, rates and invoices are paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup in the web app; optional mobile app or installable PWA
facts.dataFormat: Timesheets, projects, clients and account data live in My Hours' Microsoft Azure-hosted database in Amsterdam, Netherlands
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a straightforward cloud timesheet and reporting tool, but it has no Timeular hardware control or passive app evidence for reconstructing forgotten work.

alternatives.name: solidtime
alternatives.desc: Modern multi-user timers, clients and billable rates in one Compose stack; the desktop apps are still beta.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or self-host with the official Docker Compose examples and PostgreSQL
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted organizations, projects, clients, tasks and time entries live in PostgreSQL; deployment settings and secrets live in environment files on the host
facts.gapVsPaid: It supplies modern web timesheets and billing, but its desktop apps remain immature and it has no Timeular physical Tracker or polished automatic-activity workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting requires Docker, PostgreSQL, application-key generation, database migrations, SMTP and a TLS reverse proxy

alternatives.name: Super Productivity
alternatives.desc: A local project timer with reminders, reports and no plastic eight-sided desk ornament required.

facts.install: Install the Windows/macOS/Linux/Android app, use the web app, or add the PWA
facts.dataFormat: Tasks, notes and work logs are local-first and export as JSON; optional sync writes a JSON payload to the user's WebDAV, Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive or filesystem backend
facts.gapVsPaid: Its timer and reminders live inside a personal task manager, not a full timesheet service with Timeular's physical Tracker, team reporting and billing-oriented administration.

alternatives.name: TimeCamp Free
alternatives.desc: Unlimited people and projects get timers, auto-tracking and basic reports; app analytics, billable controls and approvals are paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup; install the Windows/macOS/Linux desktop agent for automatic computer activity
facts.dataFormat: Time entries, projects, reports and synced activity data live on TimeCamp's service-provider infrastructure, by default in an AWS data center in the United States
facts.gapVsPaid: Its free tier can track time automatically, but useful app analytics, billable controls and approvals are gated, and it offers no Timeular physical Tracker.
facts.setupBlocker: An account is required, and automatic app/site tracking needs the desktop agent plus operating-system permissions

alternatives.name: TimeTagger
alternatives.desc: A lean timeline, tags and PDF or CSV reports in one container; it is built for individuals, not payroll departments.

facts.install: Run locally with pip, or deploy the official Docker Compose image on a server
facts.dataFormat: Time records, tags and user data live in a SQLite database on the local machine or self-hosted server
facts.gapVsPaid: It is an elegant individual timeline, but lacks Timeular's physical control, native desktop capture, reminders ecosystem and team administration.
facts.setupBlocker: Remote or multi-user use requires Docker or Python hosting plus bcrypt credentials or a trusted authentication reverse proxy

alternatives.name: Toggl Track Free
alternatives.desc: Five users get fast timers, projects, tags and reports; approvals and paid-time controls cost extra.

facts.install: Hosted signup; optionally install the Windows/macOS desktop app, browser extension or mobile app
facts.dataFormat: Time entries, projects and reports sync to the Toggl Track cloud account; the private desktop Timeline activity remains on that device unless the user turns it into a time entry
facts.gapVsPaid: It has excellent timers but no Timeular physical Tracker and a weaker passive app-to-project reconstruction workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: An account is required, and passive app/site history needs the desktop app and operating-system permissions

alternatives.name: Traggo
alternatives.desc: A tiny tag-based timer with useful dashboards in one container; invoices and mobile apps never arrive.

facts.install: Run the official Docker image/Compose file, or download a Linux server binary
facts.dataFormat: Users, tags, dashboards and time spans live in a SQLite database in the mounted /opt/traggo/data directory
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a tiny tag-based web timer with no native apps, automatic activity evidence, reminders ecosystem or Timeular physical Tracker.
facts.setupBlocker: You must host the web server, persist its data volume, change the default administrator password and add TLS/reverse-proxying for internet access

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Personal plan and a personal desktop tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Timeular in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, and optional OS accessibility APIs; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: track time and focused sessions with projects and reminders using software-only controls, review patterns locally, and export a transparent activity record.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create one-click start and stop, manual entries, idle detection, tags, projects, and notes.
Keep any application-name tracking opt-in and never record window contents or keystrokes.
Add Pomodoro-style focus sessions, break reminders, and an optional allowlist blocker.
Provide daily, weekly, project, and category reports with editable corrections.
Export CSV and JSON and make the underlying event log inspectable.
Add automatic local backups and a privacy screen explaining every collected field.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out employee surveillance.
Deliberately leave out payroll and billing automation.
Deliberately leave out cross-device blocking and behavioral coaching services.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
